verses.7:2: Senhor, meu Deus, em vós esperei: * salvai-me de todos os que me perseguem, e livrai-me.
verses.7:3: {rapiat}, * enquanto não há quem {redimat}, nem quem salve.
verses.7:4: Senhor, meu Deus, se fiz isto, * se há iniquidade nas minhas mãos:
verses.7:6: Persiga o inimigo a minha alma, † e {comprehendat}, e {conculcet}, * e {deducat} a minha glória.
verses.7:7a: Levantai-vos, Senhor, na vossa ira: * e {exaltare} {finibus} dos meus inimigos.
verses.7:7b: E levantai-vos, Senhor, meu Deus, {praecepto} que {mandasti}: * e {synagoga} dos povos vos cercará.
verses.7:8b: E por causa {hanc} {regredere}: * o Senhor julga os povos.
verses.7:9b: Julgai-me, Senhor, segundo a minha justiça, * e segundo a minha inocência {superme}.
verses.7:10: {consumetur} a {nequitia} dos pecadores, e {diriges} o justo, * {scrutans}.
verses.7:11: {justum}, * que salva os retos de coração.
verses.7:12: Deus é juiz justo, forte e paciente: * {numquid} se ira todos os dias?
verses.7:13: Se não vos {conversi}, ele {vibrabit} a sua espada: * {tetendit} o seu arco, e o preparou.
verses.7:15: Eis que {parturiit}: * concebeu a dor, e {peperit} a iniquidade.
verses.7:16: Abriu {lacum}, e {effodit}: * e caiu {foveam} que fez.
verses.7:17: A sua dor {convertetur} sobre a sua cabeça: * e sobre {verticem} descerá a sua iniquidade.
verses.7:18: {confitebor} segundo a sua justiça: * e {psallam} ao nome {altissimi}.

decisions.latin: Nequándo rápiat ut leo ánimam meam
decisions.why: The verb has no named subject: after the plural ‘ex ómnibus persequéntibus me’ the Latin turns to a singular ‘he’ who is not introduced until 7:6 (inimícus). The Greek does the same (μήποτε ἁρπάσῃ). Douay-Rheims keeps a bare ‘he’; Matos Soares 1932 escapes with ‘para que ninguém’. 49:22 has the twin ‘nequándo rápiat, et non sit qui erípiat’, where the one who seizes is God. nequándo → ‘para que não’ (glossary, Ps 2:12). rápere → ‘arrebatar’ (Matos Soares 1932), which will serve 21:14 leo rápiens and 9:30b; it stays apart from erípere → arrancar. Draft 1 kept the Latin’s order (‘Para que não arrebate, como um leão, a minha alma’); the stylist heard two pauses parting the verb from its object.

options.label: Para que não arrebate a minha alma como um leão

forms.rapiat: Para que não arrebate a minha alma como um leão

options.note: Draft 2. The subject is still the Latin’s own silence: Portuguese allows a verb whose subject is understood from what precedes, the lion simile fills the gap, and the enemy is named three verses on, as in the Latin — nothing supplied, nothing resolved (rule 2). The blind reader heard ‘one of the persecutors, though which is not said’ — the Latin exactly. The order is the stylist’s: object before simile, no commas. Order is the ear’s (D2).

options.label: Para que não arrebate, como um leão, a minha alma

forms.rapiat: Para que não arrebate, como um leão, a minha alma

options.note: Draft 1: the Latin’s order (rápiat ut leo ánimam meam). Refused by the stylist: ‘as duas pausas separam o verbo do objeto’.

options.label: Para que ninguém arrebate a minha alma como um leão

forms.rapiat: Para que ninguém arrebate a minha alma como um leão

options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Fluent, but it says ‘no one’ where the Latin has a definite, unnamed ‘he’ — it turns a single hunter into a general risk.

options.label: Para que ele não arrebate a minha alma como um leão

forms.rapiat: Para que ele não arrebate a minha alma como um leão

options.note: Douay-Rheims ‘he’. A pronoun with no antecedent: in Portuguese ‘ele’ would be heard as pointing back to God, the only singular so far.

options.label: Para que o inimigo não arrebate a minha alma como um leão

forms.rapiat: Para que o inimigo não arrebate a minha alma como um leão

options.note: Names the subject of 7:6 early. Rule 2 lets a hidden subject be named, but here it spends ‘inimícus’ before the Latin does.

decisions.why: redímere has twelve verses with the present stem (grep: 7:3, 25:11, 33:23, 43:26, 48:8, 48:16, 54:19, 71:14, 102:4, 118:134, 118:154, 129:8), four of them imperatives (rédime me 25:11, 118:134, 118:154; rédime nos 43:26). The Greek here is λυτρόομαι, to ransom. Nine more have the perfect stem (30:6 redemísti me, Dómine, Deus veritátis; 70:23, 73:2, 76:15, 77:42, 105:10, 106:2, 135:24, 143:10). Not yet in the glossary.

options.label: resgate
options.note: Ruling, proposed for the glossary: redímere → resgatar. It is the ransom the Latin and the Greek name; it is plain; and it is safe at the vós imperative (‘resgatai-me’; past ‘resgatei’), where the cognate fails: ‘redimi-me’ is also ‘I redeemed myself’ (D13’s test — a good first-person sentence). Douay-Rheims ‘redeem’.

options.label: redima
options.note: The cognate. Fine in this verse; cannot serve the four imperatives (D1/D13), so it would split the word across psalms.

options.label: livre
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 (‘quem me livre’). It is liberáre’s verb, which closes the verse before (líbera me → livrai-me); two Latin verbs would become one.

decisions.why: ‘mala’ can be the object of réddidi (if I paid back evils to those who were repaying me) or of retribuéntibus (if I paid back those who repaid me evils); the Greek is open in the same way and has one verb twice (ἀνταπέδωκα τοῖς ἀνταποδιδοῦσιν), where the Latin varies réddere / retribúere. Douay-Rheims keeps the Latin order and the ambiguity: ‘If I have rendered to them that repaid me evils’. Matos Soares 1932 resolves: ‘se paguei com mal aos que mo faziam’. retribúere → retribuir (glossary family of retribútio).

options.label: Se paguei aos que me retribuíam males

forms.v5a: Se paguei aos que me retribuíam males

options.note: Ruling: the Latin’s order, which leaves ‘males’ where either verb can take it, as Douay-Rheims does. réddere → ‘pagar’ (Matos Soares 1932’s verb here): to pay back; it will serve vota réddere (‘pagarei os meus votos’, 21:26, 115:5, 115:9) and redde retributiónem (27:4, 93:2), and ‘pagai’ is safe at the vós imperative. Two verbs kept two, as the Latin has them.

options.label: Se paguei com males aos que me retribuíam

forms.v5a: Se paguei com males aos que me retribuíam

options.note: Makes ‘mala’ the object of réddidi alone. Clearer, and closes what the Latin leaves open.

options.label: Se paguei com mal aos que mo faziam

forms.v5a: Se paguei com mal aos que mo faziam

options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Drops retribúere and turns the plural into a singular; ‘mo’ is no longer said in Brazil.

options.label: Se retribuí aos que me retribuíam males

forms.v5a: Se retribuí aos que me retribuíam males

options.note: The Greek’s repetition. The Latin chose two verbs, and the Latin is what is translated (rule 1).

decisions.latin: décidam mérito ab inimícis meis inánis
decisions.why: The Latin keeps ‘inánis’ for the last word of the verse. Draft 1 did the same (‘caia eu com razão diante dos meus inimigos, vazio’). The stylist: ‘«Vazio» chega como um acréscimo depois de a frase parecer concluída; custa ligá-lo novamente a «eu»’.

options.label: caia eu vazio, com razão, diante dos meus inimigos

forms.v5b: caia eu {inanis}, com razão, {ab_inimicis} meus inimigos

options.note: Draft 2, the stylist’s order: the adjective beside the pronoun it belongs to. Order is the ear’s (D2); every word is still there. Cost: the Latin’s sting in the tail.

options.label: caia eu com razão diante dos meus inimigos, vazio

forms.v5b: caia eu com razão {ab_inimicis} meus inimigos, {inanis}

options.note: Draft 1: the Latin’s order, ‘inánis’ last. In Portuguese the adjective has no case ending to tie it back to ‘eu’, and the ear has closed the sentence before it comes.

decisions.latin: décidam mérito ab inimícis meis inánis
decisions.why: The hardest colon of the psalm. décidam is ‘may I fall’ (the Greek has an optative, ἀποπέσοιν). ‘ab inimícis meis’ is either the agent with a verb of falling — classical Latin says cádere ab áliquo for falling at someone’s hand (Lewis & Short, decido: ‘to fall down dead’, ‘to fall, fail, sink’) — or separation, which is what the Greek ἀπό says (fall away from my enemies empty-handed, i.e. come off beaten). The glossary has décidere a → ‘cair de’ (open, Ps 5:11b ‘Caiam dos seus próprios pensamentos’); here ‘caia eu dos meus inimigos’ says nothing in Portuguese. Douay-Rheims: ‘let me deservedly fall empty before my enemies’; Matos Soares 1932: ‘caia eu com razão debaixo dos meus inimigos’. mérito → ‘com razão’ (Matos Soares 1932; ‘merecidamente’ is six syllables and ‘com justiça’ would spend justítia’s word). The Latinist (draft 1, MAJOR) reads the agent only: ‘ab inimícis meis atribui aos inimigos a queda; diante dos transforma essa relação em localização’, and asks for ‘por obra dos meus inimigos’.

options.label: diante dos meus inimigos
options.note: Ruling, held against the Latinist’s major: Douay-Rheims’s ‘before’. It is the one Portuguese preposition that holds both readings — a man falls ‘diante de’ those who strike him down and ‘diante de’ those he fails against — and it states neither. The Latinist’s agent is one reading of the Latin; the Greek the Latin is calquing (ἀπο-πέσοιν ἀπό → de-cidam ab) says separation, and rule 2 forbids closing what the Latin leaves open. The blind reader, with the Portuguese alone, heard ‘que eu seja derrotado pelos inimigos’ first — so the agency the Latinist misses is in fact heard. Reported to the glossary: ‘cair de’ does not serve décidere ab + persons.

options.label: por obra dos meus inimigos
options.note: The Latinist’s fix (draft 1, major). The agent said outright with a supplied noun; it closes the Greek’s reading, goes further from the words than Douay-Rheims or Matos Soares 1932 (neither has an agent), and is stiff in the mouth. One touch away if Gustavo sides with him.

options.label: debaixo dos meus inimigos
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Adds an image (under their feet) that belongs to the next verse.

options.label: pelas mãos dos meus inimigos
options.note: The agent reading said outright. Supplies hands the Latin does not have — one verse after ‘in mánibus meis’ — and closes the Greek’s reading.

options.label: longe dos meus inimigos
options.note: The separative reading said outright (the Greek’s ἀπό). Heard as a wish to be far from them, which is the opposite of a curse on oneself.

decisions.why: The last word of the verse and its sting: empty (κενός) — empty-handed, stripped, or to no purpose. 106:9 ánimam inánem is the only other place (grep). Ps 2:1 has inánia → ‘coisas vãs’.

options.label: vazio
options.note: Ruling: the concrete word (rule 5), Douay-Rheims ‘empty’, kept last as the Latin keeps it; it will serve 106:9 ‘a alma vazia’. What it is empty of is left unsaid, as in the Latin.

options.label: de mãos vazias
options.note: The idiom. Explains, and brings in hands again.

options.label: sem esperança
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. A paraphrase.

options.label: em vão
options.note: Reads the adjective as an adverb (‘fall to no purpose’); that is the reading of ‘in vanum’, which the psalter has as a phrase of its own.

decisions.why: comprehéndere has seven verses (grep: 7:6, 9:23, 17:38, 39:13, 58:13, 68:25, 70:11), twice right after pérsequi (17:38 Pérsequar inimícos meos et comprehéndam illos; 70:11 persequímini, et comprehéndite eum). Lewis & Short: to lay hold of, seize; the Greek καταλάβοι is to overtake and seize. The Latin gives the verb no object of its own; Portuguese needs the pronoun. Not yet in the glossary.

options.label: e a prenda
options.note: Ruling, proposed for the glossary: comprehéndere → prender. It is the Latin verb’s own descendant and says exactly ‘lay hold of’; it carries every place — 9:23 ‘são presos nos conselhos’, 39:13 ‘as minhas iniquidades me prenderam’, 58:13 ‘sejam presos na sua soberba’, 68:25 ‘o furor da vossa ira os prenda’ — and in the mouth ‘e a prenda’ elides where ‘e a alcance’ and ‘e a apanhe’ pile up three a’s. Cost: the Greek’s ‘overtake’ is not heard. 70:11 comprehéndite is ‘prendei-o’ (safe; past ‘prendi’ differs).

options.label: e a alcance
options.note: The Greek’s sense (overtake), natural after ‘persiga’. Says less than the Latin’s seizing, fails 9:23 and 58:13, and ‘e a alcance’ is a run of open vowels.

options.label: e a apanhe
options.note: Holds both catch and seize; homely beside ‘persiga’ and ‘calque’, and the same vowel pile.

options.label: e se apodere dela
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 (‘apodere-se de mim’). Long, and a second idea (taking possession).

decisions.latin: et concúlcet in terra vitam meam
decisions.why: Glossary: conculcáre → ‘calcar aos pés’ (open, Ps 90:13), plainer alternative ‘pisar’. ‘in terra’ is an ablative — on the ground (the Greek has εἰς γῆν, into the ground). Draft 1 had the glossary’s ‘calque aos pés’: the stylist found ‘calque’ little used and the blind reader listed it as an unknown word — two readers, the same fault.

options.label: pise aos pés na terra a minha vida

forms.conculcet: pise aos pés na terra a minha vida

options.note: Draft 2: the stylist’s verb, the glossary row’s own plainer alternative, with ‘aos pés’ kept so that con-culcáre is still trampling and ‘pise na terra’ is not heard as treading the earth. Reported to the glossary as evidence against ‘calcar’ (Ps 90:13 has it). The stylist’s order is not taken — next option but one.

options.label: calque aos pés na terra a minha vida

forms.conculcet: calque aos pés na terra a minha vida

options.note: Draft 1, the glossary’s rendering (open, Ps 90:13). ‘Calque’ failed the stylist (‘pouco corrente’) and the blind reader (unknown word).

options.label: pise aos pés a minha vida na terra

forms.conculcet: pise aos pés a minha vida na terra

options.note: The stylist’s order, object first. Refused: ‘a minha vida na terra’ is a set phrase in Portuguese — my earthly life — so ‘in terra’ would leave the verb, where the Latin has it, and cling to the noun. That is a change of sense, not of order (D2).

options.label: calque na terra a minha vida

forms.conculcet: calque na terra a minha vida

options.note: Matos Soares 1932 (‘calque contra a terra’). ‘Calcar’ alone is to press down; the feet are what make it trampling.

decisions.latin: et glóriam meam in púlverem dedúcat
decisions.why: dedúcere is settled as ‘guiar’ (D22) — on ‘deduc me’, where God leads the way. Here an enemy brings a man’s glory down into the dust, and 21:16 has the same build (in púlverem mortis deduxísti me). ‘Guie ao pó a minha glória’ makes the enemy a kindly guide. The Greek differs (κατασκηνώσαι, make to dwell). pulvis → pó (glossary).

options.label: faça descer ao pó
options.note: Ruling for dedúcere in + a place below: the verb’s first sense in Lewis & Short, ‘to lead or bring down’, Douay-Rheims ‘bring down’. It serves 21:16 (‘me fizestes descer ao pó da morte’). D22 stands for ‘deduc me’; this is reported to the glossary as a second build, not a change.

options.label: leve ao pó
options.note: Plainer and shorter; loses the de-, and ‘levar’ will be wanted for ferre / portáre.

options.label: reduza a pó
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Another image: the glory ground to dust, not laid in it.

options.label: guie ao pó
options.note: D22’s verb. Refused here: guiding is benevolent.

decisions.latin: et exaltáre in fínibus inimicórum meórum
decisions.why: exaltáre is a passive imperative (ὑψώθητι), parallel to Exsúrge; the same form opens 20:14, 56:6, 56:12, 93:2, 107:6 (grep) — what is ruled here is a formula: ‘Exaltáre super cælos, Deus’. Glossary: exaltáre → exaltar; Exsúrge, Dómine → ‘Levantai-vos, Senhor’.

options.label: exaltai-vos
options.note: Ruling, proposed for the formula: the Portuguese pronominal form is the natural dress of a Latin medio-passive (as ‘levantai-vos’ for Exsúrge — the two imperatives then match, as ἀνάστηθι … ὑψώθητι match); it is safe (past ‘exaltei’) and sings well in ‘Exaltai-vos acima dos céus’. Cost: it can be heard as a pure reflexive, ‘exalt yourself’, where the Latin form is passive.

options.label: sede exaltado
options.note: Douay-Rheims ‘be thou exalted’: the passive to the letter. Heavier, and brings a masculine participle the Latin does not have.

options.label: mostrai a vossa grandeza
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. A paraphrase.

decisions.why: fines: the borders of a people, and so their territory (the Greek ἐν τοῖς πέρασι, at the ends). The phrase is only here (grep). This is the Latin’s reading, not the Hebrew’s ‘against the rage of my enemies’. The glossary keeps ‘confins’ for fines terræ (row términi terræ).

options.label: nos confins
options.note: Ruling: the glossary’s word for fines, which says both the edges and the lands, as the Latin does; Douay-Rheims ‘in the borders’.

options.label: nas fronteiras
options.note: The border only; a modern political word.

options.label: nos territórios
options.note: The land only; a proparoxytone and administrative.

options.label: no meio
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Not what fines says.

decisions.why: D19: præcéptum → decreto; this is one of its eight places (the Ps 2 agent tried it as ‘no decreto que ordenastes’). The Greek is ἐν προστάγματι ᾧ ἐνετείλω. ‘in’ is left as wide as the Latin’s: in, by, in keeping with.

options.label: no decreto
options.note: D19 applied, and it holds: God is asked to rise as judge in the decree he himself gave — a judicial word in a judicial psalm.

options.label: no preceito
options.note: Douay-Rheims ‘precept’. D15 gave ‘preceitos’ to justificatiónes.

options.label: segundo a lei
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 (‘segundo a lei estabelecida por ti’). ‘lei’ is lex’s, and ‘segundo’ narrows ‘in’.

decisions.why: Glossary: mandáre → ‘dar ordem’ (open, Ps 90:11), with the note that Ps 118:4 has ‘mandar’ for the sake of mandáta → mandamentos, ‘so either mandar everywhere or dar ordem except beside mandáta’. Twelve verses have the verb (grep). Here it has a noun object, the decree.

options.label: que mandastes
options.note: Ruling: ‘mandar’, the cognate, of one family with ‘mandamentos’ — evidence for the glossary’s first alternative (mandar everywhere): ‘dar ordem’ cannot take ‘decreto’ as its object. With a noun object ‘mandar’ is also ‘to send’, and the Latin verb has the same double edge (to commit, to send word), which serves 132:3b ‘ali o Senhor mandou a bênção’ and 41:9.

options.label: que ordenastes
options.note: The Ps 2 agent’s trial wording for this verse. The clearer verb; leaves the family of mandáta.

options.label: que estabelecestes
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 (‘estabelecida por ti’). It is constitúere’s verb.

decisions.latin: et synagóga populórum circúmdabit te. Et propter hanc
decisions.why: synagóga has four verses (grep: 7:7b, 81:1 in synagóga deórum, 85:14 synagóga poténtium, 105:18 in synagóga eórum). The cognate is a building in Portuguese. The neighbours: congregátio (five verses; 105:17 stands one verse before 105:18), ecclésia (ten), concílium (five; glossary ‘assembleia’, open, already colliding with ecclésia). The Greek here is συναγωγή. ‘hanc’ in 7:8b points back to it, so the pronoun’s gender hangs on the noun.

options.label: a congregação dos povos … por causa dela
options.note: Ruling, proposed as `open`: Douay-Rheims’s ‘congregation’, the Latin word for the same Greek one (syn-agogé = con-gregátio, a gathering together). It shares the word with congregátio — a merge on D15’s test: in 105:17–18, where congregatiónem and synagóga stand in neighbouring verses, the Greek has συναγωγή both times (read in consult/parallels/ps105.md), so the Latin’s variation there carries no difference of sense; the other places of congregátio (61:9, 67:31a, 73:2, 110:1) were not checked. It keeps ‘assembleia’ out of a third collision, and ‘e a congregação’ is sayable where ‘e a assembleia’ stacks three a’s. Cost: in Brazil the word is first a religious institute or a Protestant community.

options.label: a assembleia dos povos … por causa dela
options.note: The natural word, and the right one for 81:1 (‘na assembleia dos deuses’). Already the glossary’s word for concílium and the likely one for ecclésia.

options.label: o ajuntamento dos povos … por causa dele
options.note: The Greek word taken apart; free in the glossary. Today it leans to ‘a mob’, which suits 85:14 and 105:18 and not this verse, where the peoples gather round their judge.

options.label: a multidão dos povos … por causa dela
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. It is multitúdo’s (glossary, Ps 5).

decisions.why: régredi, to go back; only here in the psalter (grep). The Greek has ἐπίστρεψον, which elsewhere gives convértere → voltar. God, having risen to judge with the peoples around him, is asked to go back up on high — to his judgment seat, or to heaven.

options.label: regressai ao alto
options.note: Ruling: the cognate, plain and current, safe at the imperative (past ‘regressei’), and it leaves ‘voltar’ to convértere, which this psalm uses twice (7:13, 7:17).

options.label: voltai para o alto
options.note: Douay-Rheims ‘return thou on high’. Natural; it is convértere’s verb.

options.label: remontai ao alto
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 (‘remonta-te ao alto’). Literary.

decisions.latin: et secúndum innocéntiam meam super me
decisions.why: ‘super me’ is the Greek’s ἐπ᾿ ἐμοί carried over word for word. It can hang on innocéntiam (the innocence that is upon me — Douay-Rheims ‘in me’, Matos Soares 1932 ‘que há em mim’) or on Júdica (judge … over me). A Septuagintal oddity, of the kind the brief says to keep.

options.label: sobre mim
options.note: Ruling: the Latin’s two words, with both attachments still possible. Strange, as the Latin is strange.

options.label: que há em mim
options.note: Matos Soares 1932; Douay-Rheims ‘in me’. Smooth; settles the attachment and changes the preposition.

decisions.why: A future passive in the Latin (the Greek has an imperative, συντελεσθήτω, ‘let it be brought to an end’); DO prints consúmere, not consummáre. Douay-Rheims: ‘shall be brought to nought’; Matos Soares 1932: ‘Será consumida’.

options.label: Será consumida
options.note: Ruling: the cognate in the Latin’s tense and voice (Matos Soares 1932). Wickedness used up, burnt out.

options.label: Chegará ao fim
options.note: The Greek’s sense (come to an end), active; plainer, further from the Latin’s verb.

options.label: Seja consumida
options.note: The Greek’s mood. The Latin has a future, and the Latin governs (rule 1).

decisions.why: nequítia has four verses (grep: 7:10, 27:4, 54:16, 72:8), πονηρία here. Its neighbours: malítia (seven verses) wants ‘malícia’; iníquitas is ‘iniquidade’; malígnus is ‘malvado’ (D24). Not yet in the glossary.

options.label: maldade
options.note: Ruling, proposed for the glossary: the plain word, free, feminine like the Latin, and it leaves ‘malícia’ to malítia. 72:8 has nequítiam and iniquitátem side by side: ‘maldade … iniquidade’ holds.

options.label: malícia
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. It is malítia’s cognate, and today it is first slyness.

options.label: perversidade
options.note: Heavier; wanted for pervérsus (17:27).

decisions.why: Glossary: dirígere → dirigir (working), banned only at the vós imperative (row ‘dirígere at the vós imperative’ → endireitai). This is a future, so the ban does not reach it. The Greek is κατευθυνεῖς, to make straight.

options.label: dirigireis o justo
options.note: Ruling: the working glossary verb, in a form the ban does not touch. With a person as object it says ‘guide, steer’, which is what Douay-Rheims has (‘thou shalt direct the just’). Cost: four i’s in a row; sayable.

options.label: endireitareis o justo
options.note: The imperative’s substitute (Ps 5:9) carried into the future, for the sake of one verb. With a person as object it is to straighten someone out — a correction the Latin does not say.

options.label: encaminhareis o justo
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Good Portuguese; adds the road (caminho is via’s).

decisions.why: A participle and a nominative: either it continues ‘díriges’ with Deus as vocative (you will direct the just, you who search hearts and reins, O God — Matos Soares 1932), or it is a sentence of its own (Douay-Rheims: ‘the searcher of hearts and reins is God’). The Greek (ἐτάζων … ὁ θεός) is open in the same way. scrutári → sondar (glossary, open, which names this verse). renes: the kidneys, seat of the hidden affections — five verses (grep: 7:10, 15:7, 25:2, 72:21, 138:13).

options.label: Deus, vós que sondais os corações e os rins

forms.scrutans: Deus, vós que sondais os corações e os {renes}

options.note: Draft 2. After a second-person verb the participle is most simply its continuation, and ‘Deus’ is then a vocative, written bare as the glossary has it (no ‘ó’). ‘Vós que’ is the subject Portuguese needs (D2). The vocative comes first at the stylist’s request — left at the end it sounded ‘como uma identificação acrescentada’; order is the ear’s. ‘Sondar’ holds with hearts as its object.

options.label: vós que sondais os corações e os rins, Deus

forms.scrutans: vós que sondais os corações e os {renes}, Deus

options.note: Draft 1: the Latin’s order, the name last. Refused by the stylist.

options.label: quem sonda os corações e os rins é Deus

forms.scrutans: quem sonda os corações e os {renes} é Deus

options.note: Douay-Rheims’s build. A possible reading; it breaks the address in mid-verse and supplies a copula the other reading does not need.

options.label: sondando os corações e os rins, Deus

forms.scrutans: sondando os corações e os {renes}, Deus

options.note: The participle as a gerund: nothing supplied, both readings open. A dangling gerund before a bare noun is not sayable Portuguese.

decisions.why: Rule 5: concrete images stay concrete (bones, horn, rock, fat). The kidneys recur in 15:7 (increpuérunt me renes mei), 25:2 (ure renes meos et cor meum), 72:21, 138:13 (possedísti renes meos).

options.label: rins
options.note: Ruling, proposed for the glossary: the Latin’s organ, named. A modern ear hears anatomy first; so does a modern ear reading ‘renes’. It is one short word that serves all five verses.

options.label: entranhas
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Softer and wider; it is víscera’s word, and a proparoxytone-free gain is not needed here.

options.label: íntimo
options.note: An abstraction for an image (rule 5 forbids it).

decisions.why: No verb. Either ‘Just is my help from the Lord’ (Douay-Rheims; the Greek puts the adjective in predicate position, δικαία ἡ βοήθειά μου) or ‘My just help is from the Lord’ (Matos Soares 1932: ‘O meu legítimo auxílio vir-me-á do Senhor’). adjutórium → auxílio (glossary). This is the Latin’s reading, not the Hebrew’s ‘my shield’.

options.label: Justo é o meu auxílio vindo do Senhor

forms.justum: Justo é o meu auxílio vindo do Senhor

options.note: Draft 2. The predicate reading, with the Greek and Douay-Rheims, in the Latin’s order — ‘Justo’ first, as ‘Justum’ is, and ‘judex justus’ follows in the next verse. The stylist’s fault is taken (two ‘que’ in a row, and a pause before the mediant): a participle now hangs ‘a Dómino’ on the noun, so the only ‘que’ left is the Lord’s. His wording is not — next option but one.

options.label: Justo é o meu auxílio, que vem do Senhor

forms.justum: Justo é o meu auxílio, que vem do Senhor

options.note: Draft 1. Refused by the stylist: ‘os dois «que» encadeiam explicações e enfraquecem a afirmação’.

options.label: Meu auxílio justo vem do Senhor

forms.justum: Meu auxílio justo vem do Senhor

options.note: The stylist’s line. Refused: it makes ‘justum’ an attribute and moves the statement to ‘comes from the Lord’, where the Greek and Douay-Rheims read ‘Just is my help’; and it drops the article before the possessive (rule 5). Matos Soares 1932 reads the same way (‘O meu legítimo auxílio vir-me-á do Senhor’), so it is within D2’s outer bound — selectable.

options.label: Justo é o meu auxílio da parte do Senhor

forms.justum: Justo é o meu auxílio da parte do Senhor

options.note: No verb supplied: ‘da parte de’ for ‘a’ (the Greek παρά). Biblical and a little stiff.

decisions.why: numquid opens a question that expects ‘no’; fourteen verses (grep), five of them in a row in Ps 87. This is the Latin’s reading — a patient judge who is not angry every day — against the Hebrew’s ‘a God who is angry every day’. irásci → irar-se (glossary); per síngulos dies → ‘todos os dias’, as Ps 6:7 per síngulas noctes → ‘todas as noites’ (also 41:11, 144:2).

options.label: acaso
options.note: Ruling, proposed for the glossary: current, two syllables lighter than ‘porventura’, and it bears repeating (87:11–13). Lowercase after the asterisk, as DO prints numquid.

options.label: porventura
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. The traditional Bible word; bookish today.

options.label: será que
options.note: The spoken form. Too colloquial for the register, and it does not by itself expect ‘no’.

decisions.latin: Nisi convérsi fuéritis … Convertétur dolor ejus in caput ejus
decisions.why: The psalm has convértere twice: unless you turn (7:13), his pain will turn upon his own head (7:17) — the Greek has ἐπιστραφῆτε … ἐπιστρέψει. The glossary has convértere → voltar (open), because ‘converter’ is heard as religious conversion. In 7:13 religious conversion is what is meant (Douay-Rheims ‘Except you will be converted’; Matos Soares 1932 ‘Se vos não converterdes’), so the glossary’s reason for avoiding the cognate is absent; in 7:17 the cognate is impossible. The words ‘nisi convérsi fuéritis’ are also in the Gospel (Mt 18:3 — from memory, unverified).

options.label: Se não vos converterdes … se voltará
options.note: Draft 3, ruled by the main session (DECISIONS.md D25). The agent’s own note gives the reasons: the glossary avoids “converter” because it is heard as religious conversion, and here that is what is meant; it is the Latin’s own word (D2); Douay-Rheims and Matos Soares 1932 have it; and the blind reader found that “Se não vos voltardes” can be heard as said to God, who is “vós” in this psalter and is asked “Voltai-vos” in 6:5 — “converterdes” cannot be said to God. Cost: the echo with 7:17 (convertétur dolor ejus) is no longer heard, and convértere has two renderings. No critic has read draft 3. Matos Soares 1932 in 7:13. The expected word, and right in sense; the echo with 7:17 is lost, and the glossary verb gains a second rendering.

options.label: Se não vos voltardes … se voltará
options.note: Draft 2’s wording, by the translating agent. the glossary verb in both places, so that the turn refused in 7:13 is the turn suffered in 7:17, as in the Latin (rule 6). ‘Voltar-se’ with nothing added is as bare as ‘convérsi’: turn round, turn back, turn to God. Cost: the ear that knows the Gospel line expects ‘converterdes’. For Gustavo’s ear. Heard (draft 1): the blind reader took it first as ‘if you do not repent’ — the sense wanted — but listed a third reading the Latin does not have: since God too is ‘vós’ in this psalter, ‘Se não vos voltardes’ can be heard as said to God (whom 6:5 asks ‘Voltai-vos’); ‘ele brandirá’ at once makes God a third person and corrects it. ‘Converterdes’ could not be said to God — that is the strongest argument for option 2.

decisions.why: vibráre, to brandish (Lewis & Short: ‘to set in tremulous motion … to brandish’; of weapons also to gleam, which is what the Greek says, στιλβώσει). Only here (grep). The subject is God, from 7:12; Portuguese names him with ‘ele’ (D2).

options.label: ele brandirá a sua espada
options.note: Ruling: the verb Portuguese has for exactly this gesture. The cognate can be heard the wrong way round (next option). The blind reader listed ‘brandirá’ as unknown, yet paraphrased it rightly (‘empunhará a espada’); kept.

options.label: ele vibrará a sua espada
options.note: Matos Soares 1932, Douay-Rheims’s sense. Today ‘vibrar’ is first intransitive — the sword itself vibrating.

options.label: ele agitará a sua espada
options.note: Lewis & Short’s ‘shake, agitate’, for the blind reader, who listed ‘brandirá’ as an unknown word. Plain, and weaker than the gesture: one ‘agita’ a flag.

decisions.why: téndere arcum only here; inténdere arcum five times (grep: 10:3, 36:14, 57:8, 63:4, 77:9) — the glossary’s inténdere → atender cannot serve those. Perfects in the Latin: the bow is already bent.

options.label: armou o seu arco
options.note: Ruling, proposed for téndere / inténdere arcum: what Portuguese says of a bow made ready by bending it (Matos Soares 1932), the plainer of two faithful words (D2). ‘Armaram o arco’ serves the five places.

options.label: retesou o seu arco
options.note: The exact verb (to draw taut). Few will know it.

options.label: estendeu o seu arco
options.note: The cognate; in Portuguese it lays the bow out flat.

decisions.why: vas is a vessel and, in the plural, gear of any kind (Lewis & Short; the Greek σκεύη is the same). 2:9 vas fíguli → ‘vaso de oleiro’ (glossary); 70:22 in vasis psalmi is again ‘instruments’. ‘In eo’ → ‘nele’: in the bow, as open as the Latin.

options.label: instrumentos de morte
options.note: Ruling: Douay-Rheims’s word; the second sense of vas, which 70:22 will need too. ‘Vasos de morte’ says vases.

options.label: armas de morte
options.note: Narrower than vasa; arma is a word of its own (34:2, 45:10).

options.label: vasos de morte
options.note: One word for vas everywhere. Not understood.

decisions.why: ardéntibus cannot agree with sagíttas (accusative): it is a dative — he made his arrows for those who burn (Douay-Rheims: ‘for them that burn’; the Greek τοῖς καιομένοις) — or an ablative, with burning things. The Hebrew’s ‘he makes his arrows fiery’ is what Matos Soares 1932 prints (‘preparou as suas setas ardentes’), against the Latin. sagítta → seta (Ps 90:6). effícere → ‘fazer’: the Latin has effécit here and fecit in 7:16, the Greek ἐξειργάσατο … εἰργάσατο, kin in both.

options.label: fez as suas setas para os que ardem

forms.v14b: fez as suas setas para os que ardem

options.note: Ruling: the dative, with the Greek and Douay-Rheims. Who ‘those who burn’ are — with rage, with malice, in punishment — is left as dark as the Latin leaves it.

options.label: fez as suas setas com coisas ardentes

forms.v14b: fez as suas setas com coisas ardentes

options.note: The ablative. Possible Latin; no Vulgate-family version reads it so.

options.label: aprontou as suas setas para os que ardem

forms.v14b: aprontou as suas setas para os que ardem

options.note: Douay-Rheims ‘made ready’. A third ‘prepare’ after parávit twice; effícere is to make.

options.label: fez ardentes as suas setas
options.note: The Hebrew’s sense (Matos Soares 1932). Refused: the Latin’s case forbids it (rule 1).

decisions.why: parturíre is to be in labour (Douay-Rheims: ‘he hath been in labour with injustice’), followed — in the Latin’s odd order, kept — by conceiving and bearing. Matos Soares 1932 has ‘deu à luz’ for both partúriit and péperit. The subject changes without notice from God (7:13–14) to the sinner; the Latin names no one and neither may the Portuguese (rule 2) — Matos Soares adds ‘(o ímpio)’ in brackets. 47:7 dolóres ut parturiéntis.

options.label: sentiu as dores de parto da injustiça

forms.parturiit: sentiu as dores de parto da injustiça

options.note: Draft 2, the stylist’s line. It is what parturíre means (to be in travail; the Greek ὠδίνησεν is ‘had birth-pangs’), and the three verbs are still three. Cost, accepted: ‘dores’ now stands one colon before ‘a dor’ (dolórem), an echo the Latin’s words do not have — though its sense does, and 47:7 has the very phrase (dolóres ut parturiéntis).

options.label: esteve de parto da injustiça
options.note: Draft 1: ‘estar de parto’ is being in labour, and it kept ‘dor’ for dolórem alone. Refused by the stylist: ‘soa traduzido; a sequência «de parto da» torna a imagem mais difícil de dizer e reconhecer’. The Latinist and the blind reader had passed it.

options.label: deu à luz a injustiça
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Merges parturíre with párere in the same verse.

decisions.why: párere, to bear. Portuguese has the plain verb and the idiom.

options.label: deu à luz a iniquidade
options.note: Ruling: what is said of a birth in the register sought (Matos Soares 1932). ‘Light’ is not in the Latin, but the idiom is dead as an image.

options.label: pariu a iniquidade
options.note: The Latin’s own verb and the concrete one (rule 5); in Brazil it is said of animals, or coarsely. For Gustavo’s ear.

decisions.latin: Lacum apéruit, et effódit eum: et íncidit in fóveam quam fecit
decisions.why: Two nouns for the hole (λάκκος / βόθρος), two verbs for digging it. lacus has seven verses (grep), four of them ‘descendéntibus in lacum’ (27:1, 29:4, 87:5, 142:7b) — the pit of the dead — and 39:3 de lacu misériæ; fóvea has three (7:16, 56:7 Fodérunt … fóveam: et incidérunt in eam — a near twin — and 93:13). effódere only here; fódere in 21:17, 56:7, 93:13.

options.label: uma cova, e a cavou … no fosso
options.note: Ruling, proposed for the glossary: lacus → cova, because ‘os que descem à cova’ is what Portuguese says of the dead and the word must serve those four verses; fóvea → fosso (56:7 ‘Cavaram um fosso diante de mim, e caíram nele’). Two nouns kept two. effódere shares ‘cavar’ with fódere: they never meet, and ‘escavar’ belongs to archaeology.

options.label: um poço, e o cavou … na cova
options.note: lacus as the cistern it literally is. ‘Os que descem ao poço’ (27:1 …) would not be understood.

options.label: uma cova, e a cavou … nessa cova
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 (‘Abriu e cavou uma cova, e caiu nessa (mesma) cova’): one noun for two.

decisions.why: vertex, the crown of the head (κορυφή), set beside caput; the other place is 67:22 vérticem capílli (grep). ‘In caput … in vérticem’: one preposition twice, so ‘sobre … sobre’. Four genitives (ejus, ejus, ipsíus, ejus): Portuguese ‘a sua’ each time, the Latin’s ipsíus not pressed (Douay-Rheims does not press it either).

options.label: sobre o alto da sua cabeça
options.note: Draft 2, the Latinist’s fix (minor): vertex is the top of the head, and ‘crânio’ brought in the bone. Cost: ‘cabeça’ twice where the Latin has two nouns, and a colon three syllables over. Portuguese has no second plain word (‘cocuruto’ is comic).

options.label: sobre o seu crânio
options.note: Draft 1: a second, concrete word, which would also serve 67:22 vérticem capílli. The Latinist: it ‘perde essa precisão e introduz uma referência óssea’.

options.label: sobre a sua fronte
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. The forehead is not the vertex.

decisions.why: D5: confitéri to God → dar graças a; the coordinator names this verse as one of its places. Douay-Rheims has ‘I will give glory’, Matos Soares 1932 ‘Glorificarei’. ‘Secúndum justítiam ejus’ answers 7:9b ‘secúndum justítiam meam’: ‘segundo’ both times.

options.label: Darei graças ao Senhor
options.note: D5 applied — and it holds: thanks ‘according to his justice’ is the fitting close of a psalm that asked for judgment; the dative is kept.

options.label: Glorificarei o Senhor
options.note: Matos Soares 1932, Douay-Rheims. It is glorificáre’s verb (glossary), and loses the dative.

options.label: Louvarei o Senhor
options.note: laudáre’s verb (D5).

decisions.why: psállere is not yet in the glossary and is everywhere: twelve verses have ‘psallam’ alone (grep), and the imperative psállite many more. Lewis & Short: to play on a stringed instrument, to sing to the cithara; in Church Latin, to sing the psalms. It stands beside cantáre in one verse in 12:6b, 20:14, 103:33, 107:2 and others, so it cannot be ‘cantar’. This colon is 12:6b’s last colon word for word: whatever stands here is copied there. Draft 1 had the cognate ‘salmodiarei’: the stylist found it heavy and ‘do vocabulário especializado’, and the blind reader listed it as an unknown word.

options.label: entoarei salmos
options.note: Draft 2, proposed as `open`: the stylist’s noun (‘salmos’, the family of psalmus, as he asked) with a verb that is not ‘cantar’, so that cantábo … psallam (12:6b, 103:33, 107:2) stays two verbs: ‘cantarei ao Senhor … e entoarei salmos ao nome’. The dative is kept; ‘entoai salmos’ is safe at the vós imperative (past ‘entoei’) and bears 46:7’s fourfold psállite. Cost: two words for one; where the Latin has psalmum + a verb of its own (psalmum dícite, 65:2) the noun will be said once all the same.

options.label: cantarei salmos
options.note: The stylist’s wording. Refused: it puts ‘cantar’ in the verb, and 12:6b — this same colon, after ‘cantábo Dómino’ — would say ‘cantarei … cantarei’ where the Latin has two verbs (as the Greek has, ᾄσω … ψαλῶ).

options.label: salmodiarei
options.note: Draft 1: the cognate, one word for one, safe at the imperative (‘salmodiai’). Failed the stylist (heavy, specialised) and the blind reader (unknown word).

options.label: cantarei
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 (‘cantarei o nome’). cantáre’s verb.

decisions.why: Altíssimus → Altíssimo (glossary); DO prints the adjective lowercase here. The word is a proparoxytone and the Latin ends the psalm on the same stress (altíssimi); rule 4 would rather have the stress on the last or second-last syllable.

options.label: do altíssimo Senhor
options.note: Draft 2, from the stylist: the psalm closes on an oxytone, as rule 4 asks. Order only (D2), and ‘o altíssimo Senhor’ is as native as ‘o bom Deus’. 12:6b copies it.

options.label: do Senhor altíssimo
options.note: Draft 1: natural order and the Latin’s own final stress (altíssimi). The stylist: ‘termina o verso com duas sílabas depois da tônica, contrariando a cadência pedida’. Ps 90:1 lets ‘Altíssimo’ stand at a mediant, so this is not excluded — selectable.

options.label: do Senhor, o Altíssimo
options.note: Reads the adjective as the divine name (9:3 Altíssime). DO’s lowercase does not.

choices.7:2: The psalm begins at 7:2 (7:1 is the titulus; D7). Glossary throughout: Deus meus → ‘meu Deus’, speráre in → ‘esperar em’, salvum me fac → ‘salvai-me’, liberáre → ‘livrai-me’ (safe: past ‘livrei’); pérsequi → perseguir.
choices.7:3: ‘neque qui salvum fáciat’ → ‘nem quem salve’ (salvum fácere → salvar). ‘dum non est’ → ‘enquanto não há’ (Douay-Rheims ‘while there is no one’). 49:22 is the near twin. Order since draft 2: object before simile (decision rapiat).
choices.7:4: istud → ‘isto’ (the thing he is charged with; the titulus that named it is out, D7). The verse ends on the Latin’s colon: the oath runs on into 7:5–6.
choices.7:5: mérito → ‘com razão’ (Matos Soares 1932). Since draft 2 ‘vazio’ stands beside ‘eu’ (decision v5order). The colon stands against the Latinist’s major on ‘ab inimícis’ (decision ab_inimicis).
choices.7:6: The flex kept. Jussives (persequátur, comprehéndat, concúlcet, dedúcat) → Portuguese subjunctives without ‘que’: the self-curse opens on its verb as the Latin does. ánima mea → ‘a minha alma’, vita → ‘vida’, kept apart as the Latin keeps them.
choices.7:7a: ‘Exsúrge, Dómine’ → ‘Levantai-vos, Senhor’ (glossary formula, Ps 3:7), twice in 7:7a–7b as the Latin.
choices.7:7b: The inline marker (8a) is not reproduced. circumdáre → cercar (glossary); the future kept (circúmdabit).
choices.7:8b: The inline marker (9a) is not reproduced. propter → ‘por causa de’ (glossary). ‘júdicat’ is a present in DO’s Latin (the Greek has a future): ‘julga’.
choices.7:9b: ‘Júdica me, Dómine’ → ‘Julgai-me, Senhor’ (glossary, bare; = 25:1). ‘sobre mim’: the blind reader could attach it both ways, ‘com dificuldade’ — the Latin’s own difficulty (decision superme).
choices.7:11: ‘salvos facit’ → ‘salva’; rectus corde → ‘retos de coração’ (seven verses with this one, by grep: 10:3, 31:11, 36:14, 63:11, 96:11, 124:4).
choices.7:12: A copula supplied (‘Deus é juiz justo’; Douay-Rheims ‘God is a just judge’). pátiens → ‘paciente’ (85:15, 144:8).
choices.7:13: Plural humans are ‘vós’: ‘Se não vos voltardes’. paráre → preparar (glossary), twice (7:13, 7:14) as the Latin has parávit twice.
choices.7:15: The subject changes silently from God to the sinner, as in the Latin. dolor → ‘dor’ here and in 7:17. injustítia → injustiça, iníquitas → iniquidade, kept apart. The blind reader: the verbs with no subject ‘podem fazer o ouvinte atribuí-los inicialmente a Deus’ — so can the Latin’s; ‘injustiça’ corrects it within the colon.
choices.7:16: ‘íncidit’ read as a perfect with Douay-Rheims and Matos Soares 1932 (the Greek has a future).
choices.7:18: The second colon = 12:6b’s last colon word for word (grep): Ps 12 copies it.
choices.7:10: The first colon is the psalm’s longest (+5): two clauses in one colon, as the Latin has them. The blind reader noted that ‘rins’ may be taken literally (decision renes).

audit.note: Latin = DO Psalm7.txt, eighteen prayed verses 7:2–7:18 with DO’s split ids (7:7a, 7:7b, 7:8b, 7:9b) and two inline markers, (8a) and (9a), not reproduced. 7:6 has a flex and a mediant; every other verse one ‘*’. 7:1 is the titulus (D7). The Diurnal Monástico 1962 does not have this psalm, so no diction is borrowed from it.

Psalm-level draft from consult/parallels/ps007.md. Sense from the Vulgate family (Douay-Rheims; Matos Soares 1932 by its text layer). DO’s Portuguese not used (D12). Lewis & Short read for decido, vibro, psallo. Repeats found with ps005/grep_latin.py: 7:18b = 12:6b’s last colon word for word; 7:3 ~ 49:22 (nequándo rápiat); 7:6 pérsequi + comprehéndere = 17:38, 70:11; 7:9b Júdica me, Dómine = 25:1; 7:16 ~ 56:7; Exaltáre opens 20:14, 56:6, 56:12, 93:2, 107:6. Homograph ban checked at every vós imperative: salvai-me, livrai-me, Levantai-vos, exaltai-vos, regressai, Julgai-me are all -ar verbs and safe. Glossary rulings applied and tested: D5 at 7:18 (holds), D19 præcéptum → decreto at 7:7b (holds), scrutári → sondar (holds with corda et renes), convértere → voltar in both 7:13 and 7:17, dirígere → dirigir in the future. Places where the Latin follows the Septuagint against the Hebrew and is followed: 7:5b, 7:7a in fínibus, 7:11 adjutórium, 7:12 numquid, 7:14 ardéntibus. Departures from the glossary, each a decision: dedúcere in púlverem → ‘fazer descer’ (D22’s ‘guiar’ was made on deduc me); décidere ab + persons → ‘cair diante de’. New words proposed: redímere → resgatar, comprehéndere → prender, psállere → salmodiar, nequítia → maldade, synagóga → congregação, lacus / fóvea → cova / fosso, renes → rins, numquid → acaso, téndere arcum → armar o arco, réddere → pagar, rápere → arrebatar.

Draft 1: hard pass (ids and marks). Soft flags, all accepted: 7:2 both cola −3 and 7:4 first colon −4 (‘Senhor, meu Deus’ is four syllables for the seven of Dómine, Deus meus); 7:3 first colon +4 (‘Para que não’ for Nequándo, articles); 7:7a second colon −3; 7:10 first colon +5 (the heaviest line: ‘Será consumida a maldade dos pecadores, e dirigireis o justo’ — two clauses in one colon, as the Latin has them; with its elisions it is about twenty syllables) and second colon +3 (‘vós que’ supplied); 7:16 second colon −3; 7:17 first colon +3; 7:18 second colon +4 (‘salmodiarei’). Every cadence is oxytone or paroxytone except the last word of the psalm, ‘altíssimo’, which has the Latin’s own stress (altíssimi) — decision altissimi. No rhyme flag.

Draft 1. Two verses: 7:5 major (ab inimícis is the agent; ‘diante dos’ makes it a place), 7:17 minor (crânio is the bone, not the top of the head). Everything else passed, marks confirmed in all eighteen verses — including exaltai-vos for the passive imperative, ‘fazer descer’, ‘para os que ardem’, ‘sobre mim’, ‘voltardes’, ‘esteve de parto’ and ‘salmodiarei’.

outcomes.remark: ‘ab inimícis meis’ attributes the fall to the enemies; ‘diante dos meus inimigos’ turns the relation into a location → ‘por obra dos meus inimigos’ (MAJOR)
outcomes.reason: Held against him on purpose. The agent is one reading of the Latin; the Greek it calques (ἀποπέσοιν ἀπό) says separation, neither Vulgate-family version has an agent (Douay-Rheims ‘before’, Matos Soares 1932 ‘debaixo’), and ‘diante de’ holds both — the blind reader heard ‘defeated by the enemies’ first. His wording closes the second reading with a supplied noun. It is option 2.

outcomes.remark: ‘crânio’ loses the precision of vertex and brings in the bone → ‘sobre o alto da sua cabeça’ (minor)
outcomes.reason: Right: vertex is the crown of the head. ‘Cabeça’ now stands twice.

audit.note: Draft 1. Eight verses; best 7:4, worst 7:6. ‘O salmo tem gravidade e imagens fortes … o tratamento por vós se integra bem à oração. Não há rimas acidentais salientes.’ Five taken (three of them whole), three kept as options.

outcomes.remark: two pauses part the verb from its object → ‘Para que não arrebate a minha alma como um leão’
outcomes.reason: Order only (D2).

outcomes.remark: ‘vazio’ arrives after the sentence seems over → ‘caia eu vazio, com razão, diante dos meus inimigos’
outcomes.reason: Order only (D2); the Latin’s order is option 2.

outcomes.remark: ‘calque’ is little used, and the complements pile up before the object → ‘e pise aos pés a minha vida na terra’
outcomes.reason: The verb is taken (the blind reader did not know ‘calque’ either). The order is refused: ‘a minha vida na terra’ is ‘my earthly life’, which moves ‘in terra’ from the verb to the noun — a change of sense.

outcomes.remark: ‘mandar um decreto’ can sound like sending it → ‘no preceito que ordenastes’
outcomes.reason: ‘Preceito’ is refused outright (D19: præcéptum → decreto; ‘preceitos’ is justificatiónes’). ‘Ordenastes’ stays option 2: ‘mandar’ keeps the family of mandáta → mandamentos (Ps 118:4), the Latin verb has the same double edge, and the blind reader heard ‘o decreto que emitistes’ — the right sense. For the main session when it rules on the mandáre row.

outcomes.remark: the vocative alone at the end sounds like an afterthought → ‘Deus, vós que sondais os corações e os rins’
outcomes.reason: Order only (D2).

outcomes.remark: two ‘que’ in a row, and a needless pause before the mediant → ‘Meu auxílio justo vem do Senhor’
outcomes.reason: The fault is taken with another wording (‘Justo é o meu auxílio vindo do Senhor’). His line makes ‘justum’ an attribute against the Greek and Douay-Rheims, and drops the article before the possessive; it is option 3.

outcomes.remark: ‘esteve de parto da’ sounds translated and is hard to say → ‘sentiu as dores de parto da injustiça’
outcomes.reason: It is what parturíre says; how it is said is the ear’s (D2). Cost recorded: ‘dores’ one colon before ‘a dor’.

outcomes.remark: ‘salmodiarei’ is heavy and specialised; ‘altíssimo’ ends the verse on a proparoxytone → ‘e cantarei salmos ao nome do altíssimo Senhor’
outcomes.reason: Both faults taken: ‘salmos’ and the inversion (decision altissimi) are his. ‘Cantarei’ is refused because this colon is also 12:6b’s, where cantábo stands just before it: draft 2 has ‘entoarei salmos’.

audit.note: Draft 1, Portuguese only. Twenty-nine items and five unknown words (iniquidade ×3, calque, confins, brandirá, salmodiarei). Nearly every item is the Latin’s own range heard faithfully (7:3 the unnamed hunter, 7:5 what ‘vazio’ is empty of, 7:9b ‘sobre mim’, 7:14 ‘os que ardem’, 7:15 the silent change of subject). Two unknown words led to changes (calque → pise, salmodiarei → entoarei salmos). One item is a cost of vós and not of the Latin: 7:13 ‘Se não vos voltardes’ can be heard as said to God.

outcomes.remark: ‘em vós esperei’: put my hope in God / waited for God
outcomes.reason: Glossary (speráre in → esperar em); the same was heard in Ps 90 and is recorded in that row. The right sense was heard first.

outcomes.remark: ‘não arrebate’: one of the persecutors / another, unnamed agent
outcomes.reason: The Latin’s own silence, heard as the Latin is read.

outcomes.remark: ‘a minha alma’ (also 7:6): the spiritual soul / my life
outcomes.reason: Glossary (ánima mea → a minha alma); 7:6 sets ánimam and vitam side by side, so ‘vida’ is not free.

outcomes.remark: ‘se fiz isto’: something said before / what follows; ‘iniquidade nas minhas mãos’: guilt / ill-gotten goods
outcomes.reason: ‘istud’ points to a charge the psalm never states (the titulus that hints at it is out, D7); ‘in mánibus’ is the Latin’s image.

outcomes.remark: ‘Se paguei aos que me retribuíam males’: paid those who repaid me evils / paid with evils those who repaid me
outcomes.reason: Exactly the two readings of the Latin, which the wording was built to keep.

outcomes.remark: ‘caia eu’: be defeated / die / fall; ‘vazio’: without goods / without strength / inwardly empty
outcomes.reason: décidam and inánis are as open. ‘Defeated by the enemies’ was heard first — see decision ab_inimicis.

outcomes.remark: ‘faça descer ao pó a minha glória’: destroy my honour / end my rank / bring to death what is my glory
outcomes.reason: The Latin’s image, unexplained.

outcomes.remark: ‘nos confins dos meus inimigos’: in their territory / at its borders or far ends; ‘confins’ unknown
outcomes.reason: fines is both. ‘Confins’ is the glossary’s word (fines terræ) and lives in ‘os confins da terra’.

outcomes.remark: ‘no decreto que mandastes’: rise to carry out the decree / rise in keeping with it
outcomes.reason: ‘in’ is as wide in the Latin; neither reading is ‘sent’, the stylist’s worry.

outcomes.remark: ‘a congregação dos povos’: a gathering of peoples / a religious community — the second heard first
outcomes.reason: The cost the decision names. Peoples gathered round God as a worshipping crowd is not a wrong sense here; ‘assembleia’ is option 2.

outcomes.remark: ‘por causa dela’: the congregation / the wrath of 7:7a; ‘regressai ao alto’: to heaven / to a high seat of judgment
outcomes.reason: ‘hanc’ is no clearer (ira is feminine in the Latin too); ‘in altum’ holds both places.

outcomes.remark: ‘segundo a minha inocência sobre mim’: the innocence in me / a judgment upon me — hard to attach
outcomes.reason: Both attachments are the Latin’s; the oddity is kept on purpose, with Matos Soares’s smoothing as option 2.

outcomes.remark: ‘os rins’: bodily organs / the inmost feelings
outcomes.reason: Rule 5: the image stays; the inward sense was heard first.

outcomes.remark: ‘Justo é o meu auxílio’: the help is just / the helper is just
outcomes.reason: adjutórium is as open (the glossary’s metonymy).

outcomes.remark: ‘acaso se ira todos os dias?’: expects ‘no’ / a real question
outcomes.reason: The expected ‘no’ was heard first: ‘acaso’ does numquid’s work.

outcomes.remark: ‘Se não vos voltardes’: if you (sinners) do not repent / do not turn back / if you, God, do not turn
outcomes.reason: Repentance was heard first. The third reading is a cost of vós, not of the Latin (plural fuéritis cannot be God); ‘ele brandirá’ corrects it at once. Kept for the echo with 7:17; ‘converterdes’, which cannot be said to God, is option 2 and the note says so.

outcomes.remark: ‘ele brandirá … armou’: God / the enemy; ‘brandirá’ unknown
outcomes.reason: God was heard, rightly. ‘Brandirá’ was paraphrased rightly though listed as unknown; ‘agitará’ added as an option.

outcomes.remark: ‘nele’: in the bow / in a person; ‘para os que ardem’: to strike them / for their use; who burn literally, with passion, with fervour
outcomes.reason: ‘in eo’ and ‘ardéntibus’ are exactly as dark.

outcomes.remark: the verbs have no subject: an unjust man — or, at first, God
outcomes.reason: The Latin changes subject as silently; naming ‘o ímpio’ (Matos Soares’s bracket) would choose among peccatóres, inimícus and the ‘he’ of 7:3.

outcomes.remark: a trap / a grave
outcomes.reason: lacus is both in the psalter.

outcomes.remark: the pain he caused / the pain he feels; his evil itself / its punishment
outcomes.reason: dolor ejus and iníquitas ejus are as open.

outcomes.remark: unknown word: calque
outcomes.reason: With the stylist: ‘pise aos pés’.

outcomes.remark: unknown word: salmodiarei
outcomes.reason: With the stylist: ‘entoarei salmos’.

outcomes.remark: unknown word: iniquidade (7:4, 7:15, 7:17)
outcomes.reason: Glossary word (iníquitas → iniquidade).

audit.note: v2. Eight verses changed against draft 1. From the Latinist: 7:17 ‘sobre o alto da sua cabeça’ (was ‘o seu crânio’). From the stylist: 7:3 order (‘a minha alma como um leão’); 7:5 ‘caia eu vazio, com razão, diante dos meus inimigos’; 7:6 ‘pise aos pés’ (was ‘calque aos pés’; his order refused); 7:10 ‘Deus, vós que sondais os corações e os rins’; 7:11 ‘Justo é o meu auxílio vindo do Senhor’ (his fault, not his wording); 7:15 ‘sentiu as dores de parto da injustiça’; 7:18 ‘e entoarei salmos ao nome do altíssimo Senhor’ (was ‘salmodiarei ao nome do Senhor altíssimo’). Held against the Latinist’s major: 7:5 ‘diante dos meus inimigos’. Draft 1 is prayed.v1.json (flat text prayed.v1.vos.json, the file the three v1 critics read).

Draft 2: hard pass. New or changed soft flags, accepted: 7:15 first colon +5 (‘sentiu as dores de parto da injustiça’ — the stylist’s line for one Latin verb); 7:17 second colon +6 (‘sobre o alto da sua cabeça’, the Latinist’s fix: the longest overrun of the psalm, the price of having no second word for the head); 7:18 second colon +5 (‘entoarei salmos’), now closing on an oxytone. 7:2, 7:3, 7:4, 7:7a, 7:10, 7:16, 7:17a as in draft 1. No rhyme flag.

Draft 2 (prayed.vos.json) — the gate. One verse, the same as on draft 1: 7:5 MAJOR, ‘ab inimícis meis atribui aos inimigos a origem da queda’, fix ‘por obra dos meus inimigos’. Everything changed in draft 2 passed (the new orders of 7:3, 7:5, 7:10; ‘pise aos pés’; ‘vindo do Senhor’; ‘sentiu as dores de parto’; ‘o alto da sua cabeça’; ‘entoarei salmos ao nome do altíssimo Senhor’), and so did everything held from draft 1. The gate is therefore clean but for one major, held on purpose — the fifth place where a final text stands against the Latinist (after D10, D20, and the two of D24). No stylist or ambiguity reader has read draft 2.

outcomes.remark: ‘ab inimícis meis’ gives the enemies as the origin of the fall; ‘diante dos meus inimigos’ makes it mere presence or position → ‘por obra dos meus inimigos’ (MAJOR, second time)
outcomes.reason: Held, for the reasons in the decision: (1) the agent is one of two readings of the Latin — de-cidam ab calques the Greek ἀπο-πέσοιν ἀπό, ‘fall away from’ — and rule 2 forbids closing the other; (2) neither Vulgate-family version has an agent: Douay-Rheims ‘fall empty before my enemies’ is the wording kept, Matos Soares 1932 has ‘debaixo dos’; (3) the blind reader, given the Portuguese alone, heard ‘que eu seja derrotado pelos inimigos’ first, so the origin the Latinist misses is heard; (4) his fix supplies a noun (‘obra’) the Latin does not have. It is option 2 of the decision, one touch away.

audit.note: v3, by the main session under Gustavo’s delegation (DECISIONS.md D25): 7:13 “Se não vos voltardes” → “Se não vos converterdes”. One word; no critic re-run. The echo wording stays selectable.
